w: What's tested The molecular associations he said you need ("you do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined"): t(14;18) and BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, t(11;14) and cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma ("if you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma"), t(8;14) and MYC in Burkitt lymphoma, t(9;22) and the Philadelphia chromosome in CML, and t(15;17) and PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia The categories ("I want you to know generally kind of what category things are"): which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid; and how Hodgkin lymphoma differs from non-Hodgkin lymphoma Acute leukemia: blasts are the hallmark, and more than 20 percent blasts makes the diagnosis ("that's our threshold"), any count with a defining genetic abnormality; Auer rods mean a myeloid blast; AML in adults, ALL in young children; and the two acute leukemias "you need to know": acute promyelocytic leukemia (DIC, and an excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia in the mouth Chronic myeloid leukemia, "the main chronic leukemia that you need to know": the Philadelphia chromosome, every stage of maturation in the blood, imatinib; and CLL/SLL, one disease of small mature B cells with smudge cells What a dentist sees: swollen gums from leukemia ("you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia"), bleeding gums, Burkitt lymphoma in the jaw, the palate destroyed by NK/T-cell lymphoma, and marginal zone lymphoma in the salivary glands ("the one you guys are going to experience the most"); and the B symptoms, "really high-yield clues" of lymphoma What he said you don't need: the CD markers and the flow cytometry details ("don't waste your time learning that kind of stuff"), the AML subtypes, the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes, and the ALL details beyond who gets it Dr. Sam Borak gave Lecture 20 on Tuesday, November 17, at 2 pm, building on Dr. Herr's lecture on the blood cells the hour before. His deck, "Lymphoma/Leukemia", starts with the blood cells and how a lymphoma is diagnosed, covers leukemia in general and the bone marrow exam, walks through the major lymphomas one at a time, and ends with chronic myeloid leukemia and the acute leukemias. He opened by telling the class not to worry about the amount of detail: "Don't freak out about this lecture. There's obviously a lot of information. ... What you really need to know are going to be more of the basic." The detail is there so you see how a diagnosis is made. He closed the same way: "you don't need to know the nitty-gritty details", only each disease's category and its molecular association. These notes follow the recording and slides. His two objectives slides are the best guide to the exam: nearly every disease below has its own objective. Both say you don't need the individual markers (CD20, CD5, CD34, CD117, CD3 and the rest), and the leukemia slide adds that you don't need every type of acute leukemia, only the ones he discusses. Aloud he said the same more than once. Of the markers: "Do not waste a second learning what these antigens are. I just want you to understand the concept." Of the AML and ALL subtype lists: "you don't need to know any of these actual things, that's just to illustrate the concept." And at the end: "You don't need to know the flow cytometry stuff, CD5, CD33." How blood cells mature All blood cells come from the hematopoietic stem cell in the marrow, which can renew itself or differentiate. It gives rise to two lines: the myeloid line (red cells, platelets, granulocytes such as neutrophils, and monocytes) and the lymphoid line (B cells, T cells and NK cells). Leukemias and lymphomas are cancers of these cells, and each tends to look like, and carry the markers of, the normal cell it comes from. He said any of these cells can become a leukemia or lymphoma, but in practice it is the white cells: the granulocytes, which he also called the myeloid cells (neutrophils and monocytes), become leukemias for the most part, and the lymphoid cells (B cells, T cells and, less commonly, NK cells) become lymphomas or leukemias. Activated B cells become plasma cells, which make antibodies and have neoplasms of their own; the antibodies, and molecules on the cells' surface such as CD4 and CD8, help make the diagnosis. He came back to maturation when he turned to leukemia, calling it "one of the important concepts". The cells go through steps of maturation in the marrow as they acquire their function, and the neutrophil line, which his objectives ask for, shows it best: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and finally the segmented neutrophil, or PMN. The myeloblast is the youngest cell: very fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli and darker blue cytoplasm. In the promyelocyte the chromatin is still fine, the cytoplasm is less dark, and granules appear. In the myelocyte the chromatin turns clumped and coarse, the nucleus starts to indent, and the cytoplasm is less blue. In the band the nucleus is indented even more and the cytoplasm turns pink, and in the segmented neutrophil the nucleus is pinched into lobes. Only the neutrophils are released into the blood. (Aloud he went from the myelocyte straight to the band; his slide puts the metamyelocyte, with its kidney-shaped nucleus, between them.) In leukemia that maturation doesn't happen: the cells get stuck at the early stages, and blasts increase in the marrow and often the blood. "You should not have blasts in your blood. That is an abnormal finding, except in basically newborns." The lymphoid line has the same idea with fewer steps: under the microscope there are just immature and mature lymphoid cells. Acute leukemia is a disease of blasts; chronic myeloid leukemia fills the blood with the later, maturing stages; and in acute promyelocytic leukemia, maturation stops at the promyelocyte. The lymphatic system and what a lymphoma is The lymphatic system is the lymphatic vessels, the lymph nodes, the lymphoid organs, lymphatic tissue and the lymph itself. It produces immune cells and removes excess fluid from the body. He described nodes all through the body, near the surface and deep, joined by lymphatics, plus the spleen and lymphoid tissue in organs such as the lung and the GI tract, and said a lymphoma can arise in any of them, "pretty much anywhere in your body". A lymphoma is a blood cancer that starts in the lymphatic system and affects the lymphocytes, the white cells at the center of the immune system. The key practical point: the diagnosis requires sampling of tissue, such as a lymph node or the bone marrow. A blood count or a scan can raise the suspicion, but the tissue makes the diagnosis. (CLL, which lives in the blood, is the one he teaches that is diagnosed from a blood count.) The tissue can come from a biopsy or from excising the whole node, which he prefers, because a whole node shows features a biopsy may miss. What makes you suspect it: enlarged nodes you can feel near the surface, although enlarged nodes are often not lymphoma (reactive and infectious causes, and immune disorders such as lupus, enlarge them too); tiredness, itching, repeated infections, and bruising and bleeding; or swollen nodes found on imaging done for another reason. The B symptoms He called the B symptoms "really high-yield clues that this person is somebody you should be concerned about lymphoma": A fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher with no obvious cause Night sweats that soak the bedding and clothes: drenching sweats that make you change the sheets, not light ones Unexplained weight loss of at least 10 percent of body weight over the past 6 months Other things, such as tuberculosis, can cause B symptoms too, so the tissue still has to be sampled. Watch how often each lymphoma brings them: B symptoms are uncommon in follicular lymphoma and rare in MALT lymphoma; DLBCL can bring them, and peripheral T-cell lymphoma usually does; and in classic Hodgkin lymphoma they appear in about 20 percent of localized and 70 percent of advanced disease. The tissue: H and E, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry He set a normal lymph node beside a pathologic one. To the eye, a normal node is well circumscribed and rubbery; a lymphoma node is fleshy and plump, not circumscribed. Under the microscope a normal node has B-cell areas in its outer part, the cortex, with primary follicles and germinal centers, T-cell areas deeper in, and open (patent) sinuses between them, where the macrophages live and the lymphocytes pass in and out: patent sinuses are a clue that the node is benign. In a lymphoma the architecture is altered, or effaced: replaced by tumor cells, often one monotonous population. The lab reads the tissue three ways: the routine H and E stain for morphology; immunohistochemistry, antibodies that stain proteins in the section; and flow cytometry, which reads living cells one at a time in suspension. The H and E, purple and red, gives the baseline: normal or abnormal. If it looks abnormal, the extra studies ask whether it is a lymphoma and which one. Immunohistochemistry is an antibody to part of the cell that turns it brown: one stain lights up B cells, another looks for something abnormal on them. He placed the T cells in the area under the cortex, which he called medullary; histology texts, and Lecture 19, name the T-cell zone the paracortex, between the cortex and the medulla. No question here depends on the name. That is why the specimen handling matters. When you collect the specimen, don't put it in formalin: formalin fixes the cells, and flow cytometry needs them fresh. It may need a special medium, such as RPMI or Hanks's solution. He called flow cytometry "one of the most important tests that I do", for lymphomas and leukemias alike. Each cell type carries its own collection of antigens on its surface, so labeling millions of cells with antibodies tells whether they are B cells, T cells or myeloid cells, whether they are mature or immature (blasts), and whether something is on the surface that shouldn't be there, or missing that should be. It also gives each cell's size (a monocyte is bigger than a lymphocyte) and granularity (granulocytes have granules, lymphocytes don't). His example of something abnormal: the light chains kappa and lambda. Each B cell carries only one of them, and a normal node has both, about 3 kappa to 1 lambda. A lymphoma's cells all come from one abnormal cell, so they show only kappa or only lambda: "that's a clue that I'm looking at something that's what we call clonal." On the slides, flow cytometry detects proteins on the cell membrane, the cell surface markers, with polyclonal or monoclonal antibodies stained by an immunofluorescent method. A laser passes through each cell, and the scattered light tells two things: forward (low-angle) scatter indicates the cell's volume or size, and side scatter estimates its complexity or granularity. A granular cell such as a promyelocyte scatters a lot of light to the side; a small lymphocyte scatters little either way. His slide groups the markers into myeloid (CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO), B-lymphoid (CD10, CD19, CD22, CD79a) and T-lymphoid (CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7, CD4, CD8). He said: "You do not need to know this. Do not waste a second learning what these antigens are." No question asks for one. What to know is the idea: a lymphoma or leukemia carries the markers of the normal cell it comes from, so flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry show its lineage. Classifying lymphoma Lymphoma is classified on many parameters together: the clinical presentation, imaging, and a range of laboratory tests. No single test decides it, although morphology remains the key component, with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry playing a major role. Usually the answer is a B-cell or a T-cell lymphoma, and each resembles the normal cell it arises from, "except for this one or two things that are different" on the stains or flow cytometry. The slides follow the World Health Organization classification. He tied each lymphoma to its normal counterpart, the place where that cell matures. In the lymph node: the germinal centers give follicular lymphoma; the mantle zone just around them gives mantle cell lymphoma; and the marginal zone around the mantle gives marginal zone lymphoma. The bone marrow holds the immature cells, so the leukemias of immature cells arise there; the thymus does the same for T cells and the T-cell lymphomas. The vast majority of lymphoid neoplasms, 85 to 90 percent, are of B-cell origin. The rest are T-cell neoplasms, and tumors of NK-cell origin are rare. Lymphoma in the eye, the head and neck, and the mouth Lymphoma can arise outside the nodes, and his slides show several sites near your work. Ocular adnexal lymphoma involves the orbit, eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal gland or lacrimal sac. Inside the eye there is vitreoretinal and uveal lymphoma. He described the look: puffy eyes, with a swollen, salmon-colored look at the side of the eye where the adnexa are, and a mass on imaging that needs a biopsy. Names such as ocular adnexal or vitreoretinal lymphoma only say where the lymphoma is; the biopsy gives the diagnosis that decides treatment. These lymphomas cause a painless decrease in vision or floaters; patients without symptoms are often found on eye screening; and when the brain is involved, personality changes and altered mental status are common. In the head and neck, lymphoma can involve the tonsils (part of Waldeyer ring, the ring of lymphoid tissue around the throat), and the oral mucosa and gums. He said very swollen tonsils, bright (metabolically active) on a PET scan, call for a biopsy or excision: lymphoma wipes out the tonsil's germinal centers with one monotonous population of similar cells. In the gums, lymphoma is often not a mass but a plaque-like lesion, sometimes ulcerated, and on biopsy the tumor cells replace the connective tissue under the epithelium. His slides also cite a study of oral lymphomas in people with and without HIV. Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin lymphoma He set the two broad categories side by side, and the study guide asks for the difference. When found Usually localized Usually widespread Where it starts Central nodes you can't see: in the chest, by the heart, in the lungs, or possibly the abdomen Peripheral nodes, or outside the nodes Spread Contiguous: from one node to the node next to it Can be non-contiguous: a node above the diaphragm and one below, with the node between them not enlarged Outside the nodes Uncommon Much more common Peripheral blood Never involved Can be involved The tumor cells A few scattered, very abnormal, bizarre cells, so it can be tricky to diagnose Look very much like normal lymphocytes, so the tests are put together Treatment ABVD Often CHOP His slide on classic Hodgkin lymphoma adds that more than 70 percent of early-stage patients present with enlarged cervical or supraclavicular nodes, and more than 60 percent with mediastinal disease; aloud he stressed that it begins in the central nodes of the chest. Both put it above the diaphragm, and no question's key depends on which nodes come first. The drug names behind ABVD and CHOP were on his slide; he didn't go through them. Staging He said staging is based on whether one site or several are involved, whether they are above or below the diaphragm, or on both sides, whether there are any extranodal or extralymphatic sites, or whether the disease is disseminated: "that's the stage 4 disease, and that's the most aggressive." His slide shows the Ann Arbor staging system as a chart. In the standard system, stage I is one lymph node region; stage II is two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm; stage III is nodes on both sides of the diaphragm; and stage IV is widespread involvement of organs outside the lymphatic system, such as the bone marrow or liver. The letter B after a stage means the patient has B symptoms, and A means none. The staging slide is a picture, so stages I to III above are the standard Ann Arbor chart (Robbins) rather than his words; he named only the criteria and stage 4. No question's key depends on stages I to III. What leukemia is Leukemia is a malignant disease of the hematopoietic tissue in which neoplastic blood cells replace the normal bone marrow and peripheral blood elements. The neoplastic cells are usually white cells; less common variants involve the red cell (erythroid) or platelet (megakaryocyte) lines. Leukemia frequently starts in the bone marrow and can extend to the reticuloendothelial system (the spleen, liver and lymph nodes) and to other tissues. Untreated, it is fatal. His short version: "lymphoma generally involves lymph nodes. Leukemia generally involves the bone marrow and the blood." Leukemias of the red cells, megakaryocytes, basophils or eosinophils exist but are rare, and he didn't cover them. Its clinical features come two ways. The symptoms are mostly those of marrow failure, "and particularly anemia": the normal cells are replaced by the abnormal ones, usually blasts, so the work of the normal cells isn't done. Marrow failure, as the leukemic cells crowd out normal blood-making: anemia, with fatigue, malaise and pallor; bruising and bleeding from too few platelets; and fever and infections from too few working white cells. Organ infiltration, as the leukemic cells grow in tissues: bone and joint pain from the expanding marrow ("a significant finding that should point you toward leukemia"); splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy; neurologic symptoms when the central nervous system is involved; and gingival hypertrophy and oral lesions. "For you guys, an important one": "you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia that's not detected." For the dentist, both sides show in the mouth: pale mucosa, bleeding gums and petechiae from marrow failure, and swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them. The swollen gums of acute monocytic leukemia come up again near the end of the lecture. The bone marrow exam It is often found on a blood count, done for symptoms or during a hospital stay: the counting instrument sorts the blood's cells into areas, blasts fall in their own area, and many cells there flag a possible leukemia. A peripheral blood smear checks for blasts, and if they are there, the patient needs a bone marrow biopsy. Leukemia is diagnosed from the blood smear and the bone marrow. The marrow is sampled two ways, usually at one sitting: an aspirate, liquid marrow drawn through a needle and smeared on slides to read the individual cells, and a core biopsy, a small cylinder of bone and marrow, taken with a big needle, that keeps the marrow's architecture and shows how cellular it is. The aspirate separates the cells so their morphology can be read. The patient is anesthetized, so it isn't painful. The sternum gives an aspirate only, never a core, because the heart lies right below. Posterior iliac crest Biopsy and aspirate Sternum Aspirate only Tibia Aspirate only, in small children One marrow exam fills a folder of slides: a peripheral blood smear, "crush" and "push" marrow smears, a touch imprint of the core, a clot section of the aspirated particles, and the core biopsy. A normal marrow holds every line (red cells, white cells and megakaryocytes); in leukemia or lymphoma they are replaced by one cell type, the neoplastic cells. Acute versus chronic leukemia His two comparison slides set acute leukemia beside chronic leukemia; his chronic column is chronic myeloid leukemia. Who Usually children and the young Usually middle-aged and older Onset Rapid Insidious Course if untreated Less than 6 months 2 to 6 years Cells Immature cells: blasts Mature cells Blasts More than 20 (up to 95) percent of the marrow; more than 5 (up to 95) percent of the blood Fewer than 20 percent, in marrow and blood White count Usually increased, from the blasts, but variable Increased Anemia Mild to severe Mild Platelets Low to very low Normal to increased early, then decreased Organs Mild organomegaly Prominent organomegaly Treatment Chemotherapy, bone marrow transplant Chemotherapy, possibly a transplant Death Infection or bleeding Infection or bleeding Diagnosis Blood smear, marrow exam, stains, flow cytometry, cytogenetics Blood smear, marrow, cytogenetics (the Philadelphia chromosome) Aloud: in acute leukemia the key finding is blasts, increased in the marrow and often the blood. The white count is usually up, but it can be down; the red cells are low, causing anemia; and the platelets are low, "usually pretty severely low"; sometimes organs are enlarged. In chronic myeloid leukemia the blasts must be under 20 percent, "usually much less, if any at all"; the white count is high; anemia and low platelets can come, but milder; and the organs can be enlarged. He noted that the chronic column is chronic myeloid leukemia: chronic lymphocytic leukemia "is a little different". The thread through it: acute leukemia is blasts that don't mature, filling the marrow fast, so the other lines fail fast; chronic leukemia is cells that still mature, so the count climbs slowly, the spleen and liver fill up, and the platelets hold up until late. His acute column says "usually children and the young", but he corrected it aloud: "usually seen in children, but that's really more for ALL. For AML, those are usually more seen in adults" (median age 65). ALL is the acute leukemia of young children, and AML the acute leukemia of older adults. Classifying the acute leukemias There are two broad categories of acute leukemia. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The older system split it into subtypes M0 through M7 by the type of cell differentiation (minimal differentiation, monocytic and the rest); the WHO now classifies some types by their common genetic abnormalities. He said you don't need the subtypes: "that's just to illustrate the concept." Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The WHO divides it by genetic abnormality, and into precursor B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell (T-ALL) types. The number his objectives ask for is the blast threshold. He gave two ways to diagnose AML. With a specific cytogenetic abnormality, "you can diagnose AML right away. You don't even have to have 20% blasts." Without one, the blasts must be more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow: "That's our threshold for making the diagnosis." If the blood shows more than 20 percent, acute leukemia can be diagnosed from it; if it shows only a few, the marrow is examined. Fewer blasts than that, in a patient with abnormal counts, point to something else, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome (later in these notes). He and his slide both say "greater than 20 percent"; the WHO wording is 20 percent or more. Either way, the number to know is 20, and no question turns on the difference. Aloud he added a few points to the table below: AML is relatively rare in children; ALL is usually seen at 1 to 5 years of age, with a particularly poor prognosis under 1 year; AML's blasts have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and may or may not hold Auer rods: "If you see Auer rods, that tells you that you're looking at a myeloid blast. Lymphoid blasts do not have Auer rods." The gonads, as a site outside the marrow, are more specific to ALL, and flow cytometry tells the two apart, by markers you don't need. Who Common in adults (median age 65); relatively rare in children Common in children: highest at 1 to 5 years, peak at 2 to 3; poor prognosis under 1 year; less common in adults Blood Anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; myeloblasts (20 to 95 percent) Anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; lymphoblasts Blast size Medium to large, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio Small to medium Cytoplasm Moderate, with granules, and Auer rods Scant, no granules Nucleus Fine chromatin, distinct nucleoli Fine chromatin, indistinct nucleoli Outside the marrow Spleen, liver (lymph nodes, CNS) Nodes, spleen, liver, CNS, gonads Marrow Myeloid-to-erythroid ratio usually high Not on his slide Auer rods Can be present Never: Auer rods exclude ALL The rule that settles a smear: Auer rods exclude ALL. Find one, and the blast is myeloid. Indolent and aggressive lymphomas He sorted the lymphomas he went through one at a time two ways: indolent (slow-growing, taking a long time to cause symptoms) or aggressive (fast-growing, presenting acutely), and B-cell or T-cell. At the end he asked for exactly this: "I want you to know generally kind of what category things are. Which of these things are B-cell lymphoma? Which of these things are T-cell lymphoma?" B-cell CLL/SLL, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma T-cell or NK-cell Mycosis fungoides Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, Sézary syndrome, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma Classic Hodgkin lymphoma and the plasma cell neoplasms (tumors of the B-cell line) he took as groups of their own. He called mantle cell lymphoma "another small indolent B-cell lymphoma"; many textbooks count it among the more aggressive ones. No question's key depends on where it falls. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) CLL/SLL is a lymphoma of small, mature B cells. It is one disease with two names, depending on where it is: the same neoplastic B cell with different presentations. When only the blood is involved it is CLL; when only a lymph node, SLL; when both, CLL/SLL. (Its cells carry markers, CD5 and CD23; "you don't need to know that, just understand the concept.") CLL is diagnosed from the blood: a B-cell count of at least 5 times 10 to the 9th per liter (5,000 per microliter), with the typical look and markers. SLL is diagnosed from tissue: an enlarged organ, such as a lymph node over 15 millimeters, infiltrated by the same cells, with fewer than 5 times 10 to the 9th circulating B cells per liter. Below that blood count, with no tissue disease, a clone of these cells is a pre-neoplastic process, monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, which he said is found with flow cytometry. Who and how: the median age at diagnosis is 70 or older, and a family history of CLL is a risk factor. It may cause no symptoms at first and be found only by a lymphocytosis on a routine count, or by enlarged nodes or spleen. When it does cause symptoms, they are cytopenias (anemia, low platelets and, rarely, low neutrophils, from marrow infiltration or from autoimmune destruction), recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. The infections come from hypogammaglobulinemia, too little normal antibody, and from defective cellular immunity, the reason he gave aloud. He said they are often in the hospital for something else when a white count full of lymphocytes is found. The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes that have burst apart as the smear is made. "That's a clue right away, I'm looking at that, I'm thinking CLL." The marrow can be involved in various patterns, which he said you don't need to know. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers. Its course: despite much better outcomes since targeted therapies arrived, CLL/SLL remains largely incurable, with a slow but progressive course. The markers on his CLL slides (CD19, CD5, CD23 and dim CD20, without CD10) are the ones he said you don't need. The idea he wanted: normal B cells don't carry CD5, so B cells that do are a clue to a neoplasm, but other B-cell lymphomas, such as mantle cell, carry it too. Follicular lymphoma Follicular lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma that grows, at least in part, in a follicular pattern: crowded, back-to-back follicles fill the node. He said germinal centers in the cortex are normal, but "if you see a bunch of these germinal centers back-to-back, that's a sign that you're looking at follicular lymphoma." It is an indolent small B-cell lymphoma from germinal center B cells, and it makes up 10 to 20 percent of all lymphomas. The event that starts it is the translocation between chromosomes 14 and 18, t(14;18), found in 85 to 90 percent of cases. It moves the BCL2 gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene, IGH, so BCL2 is switched on all the time (his slide: "constitutive expression of BCL2"). BCL2 blocks apoptosis, so the cells live on instead of dying. The neoplastic follicles stain for BCL2, which helps separate them from reactive follicles. He said seeing the translocation helps make the diagnosis. Most patients already have widespread disease when it is found: nodes both near the surface and deep in the chest and abdomen, and an enlarged spleen; the marrow is involved in 40 to 70 percent (he said fairly commonly), and occasionally the blood. Yet patients are often asymptomatic, and B symptoms are uncommon. It is indolent: the median survival is more than 17 years with current treatment. But it keeps progressing over time, with no plateau in the survival curves, and the prognosis is closely tied to how far it had spread at diagnosis. Mantle cell lymphoma Mantle cell lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma from the mantle zone of the lymphoid follicle, the rim of small B cells around the germinal center. Its cells are small to medium-sized, with slightly irregular nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. He said the translocation "tells me right away, I'm looking at mantle cell lymphoma. Nothing else in the lymphomas will do that." Its cells carry CD5, like CLL/SLL's, so he needs another marker to tell them apart: cyclin D1, found by immunohistochemistry, not flow cytometry. "If you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1, you would know this is mantle cell lymphoma." Patients are older, with a median age of 68 to 69. Most present with enlarged peripheral lymph nodes, and the spleen and marrow are commonly involved. It used to be considered incurable; with current treatment, he said, the survival has increased dramatically: the median survival has risen from 3 years to more than 5 to 10, and some patients may be cured. Marginal zone lymphoma and MALT lymphoma He called it "the one you guys are going to experience the most": the last of the low-grade B-cell lymphomas. Marginal zone lymphoma comes in a nodal form and an extranodal one: extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, called EMZL or MALT lymphoma. It is an indolent B-cell lymphoma that arises outside the nodes from marginal zone B cells, often on the ground of a chronic inflammatory disorder: long inflammation keeps lymphocytes dividing in a tissue, and in time a clone escapes. The common sites are the stomach, the ocular adnexa, the salivary glands, skin, lung, breast, thyroid and thymus. Patients have symptoms from a mass, or none at all and it is found by chance; B symptoms are rare. The associations are the testable part. Aloud he named the stomach with H. pylori, the ocular adnexa with Chlamydia psittaci, and the autoimmune disorders Sjögren syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis; his slide adds the skin and Borrelia. Stomach Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection Skin (primary cutaneous) Borrelia burgdorferi Ocular adnexa Chlamydia psittaci Salivary gland Sjögren syndrome, which commonly comes first Thyroid Hashimoto thyroiditis, which commonly comes first Because infection drives some of these, a proportion respond to antibiotics. For the dentist, the salivary one matters: in a patient with Sjögren syndrome, a parotid that starts to enlarge should be checked for lymphoma. Under the microscope, atypical small to medium-sized lymphoid cells efface the tissue's architecture, often with lymphoepithelial lesions (tumor cells invading the gland's or the mucosa's epithelium), which he called the key finding. Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry help less here than in the other lymphomas. It is indolent: local recurrence, relapse in other MALT sites and spread to nodes can happen, but the prognosis is very good: the overall survival is about 90 percent at 5 years and 80 percent at 10. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is medium-sized to large B cells growing in a diffuse sheet. A cell counts as large when its nucleus is the size of a macrophage's nucleus or bigger, or more than twice the size of a small lymphocyte's nucleus; he put it as cells more than twice the size of a small lymphocyte, and said the large cells are "really the key thing to making a diagnosis". Compared with the low-grade B-cell lymphomas, the cells, the nuclei and the nucleoli are all bigger. It is the common one: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas. Most patients present with nodal disease, but 30 to 40 percent have disease only outside the nodes at diagnosis: the GI tract (stomach and ileocecal region), the head and neck (salivary glands, thyroid, ocular adnexa), bone, liver, kidney and adrenal gland. The typical story is a rapidly enlarging node or mass, at one site or several, with or without B symptoms; he said it grows more rapidly than the indolent lymphomas, can be anywhere, including the salivary glands and the ocular adnexa, and more often brings B symptoms. Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry confirm the B cells, and little else is needed. Its cause is unknown in most cases; risk factors include genetic features, immune dysregulation, and viral, environmental or occupational exposures. It can arise de novo, with no low-grade lymphoma before it, or by transformation of an indolent B-cell lymphoma, such as CLL/SLL. After R-CHOP (rituximab with combination chemotherapy), the 5-year progression-free and overall survival are both about 70 percent. Burkitt lymphoma Burkitt lymphoma is a mature, aggressive B-cell lymphoma of medium-sized cells with basophilic (blue) cytoplasm and a very high proliferation index. He called it "a very aggressive lymphoma". Its cells double so fast that patients usually present with a high tumor burden, widespread disease and rapidly growing tumors, most often outside the nodes. Its primary genetic event is the translocation between chromosomes 8 and 14, t(8;14), in 80 percent of cases: it moves MYC, a gene that drives cell growth and division, next to the IGH locus. There are three clinical forms, and his objective names the first two. He said both are seen in children. Endemic Equatorial Africa and Papua New Guinea, where it is the most common childhood cancer More than 90 percent Traditionally the mandible, maxilla and other facial bones; recent reports often describe the abdomen Sporadic Elsewhere in the world; less common in children About 20 percent Abdomen, orbit, Waldeyer ring, gingiva, thyroid, ovary, testis, breast Immunodeficiency-associated Most often with HIV Not on his slide Not on his slide The site symptoms matter in a dental school: altered vision, a blocked nose, enlarged tonsils, and dental or jaw pain, often with loss of teeth, along with abdominal masses (ileocecal lesions, retroperitoneal nodes), kidney lesions and testicular masses. He mentioned the blocked nose and the enlarged tonsils, and showed an endemic Burkitt tumor of the jaw. When he introduced the two forms, his words swapped them once: he called the sporadic type the EBV-associated one, said the endemic type is less often associated with EBV, and put the sporadic type in Africa and New Guinea, in the jaw. A minute later he called the jaw tumor he showed endemic Burkitt. His slide and the textbooks (Robbins, the WHO) agree with that: the endemic form is the African one, in the jaw, linked to EBV in more than 90 percent; the sporadic form is linked in about 20 percent. These notes follow the slide, and no question's key depends on which form carries EBV more often. Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern, which he compared to Van Gogh's painting and called "the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis". With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. He said that is why the diagnosis matters: the chemotherapy works. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma He said the main Hodgkin lymphoma is classic Hodgkin lymphoma: "You don't need to know the non-classical." It is different from the rest. The tumor cells are a small fraction of the mass, sparse and very large, embedded in a reactive background rich in immune cells. They are the Hodgkin cells (one nucleus) and the Reed-Sternberg cells (two or more nuclei), together called HRS cells. The classic Reed-Sternberg cell has two nuclear lobes, each with a prominent, eosinophilic (pink) nucleolus, which gives it an owl's-eye look. "That's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells." Stains such as CD30 and CD15 light them up, but the markers aren't needed. His slide's sentence about where it comes from is missing a word ("a neoplasm derived from characterized by"), and he didn't say it aloud. The standard answer (Robbins, WHO) is that HRS cells come from germinal-center B cells; no question asks. How it presents, and how that differs from non-Hodgkin lymphoma (the table earlier in these notes), is one of his objectives. Aloud he said it usually doesn't involve sites outside the nodes, and that it starts centrally and may eventually reach the peripheral nodes. His slide: classic Hodgkin lymphoma mainly involves lymph nodes, with a striking preference for nodes above the diaphragm: more than 70 percent of patients with early-stage disease present with enlarged cervical or supraclavicular nodes, more than 60 percent have mediastinal involvement, and fewer than 5 percent have disease only below the diaphragm. The nodes are painless and firm, and the disease involves contiguous node groups, one to the next. Disease starting outside the nodes (skin, GI tract, Waldeyer ring, CNS) is rare. B symptoms appear in about 20 percent of localized and 70 percent of advanced disease. A rare but distinctive symptom: pain in the affected nodes after drinking alcohol. Its cause is unclear, but in EBV-positive cases there is strong evidence that latent EBV infection drives the malignant change. More than 80 percent are cured with modern combination chemotherapy, with radiotherapy for some. The example he showed was the nodular sclerosis type: nodules of lymphocytes separated by bands of fibrosis, with the large Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells. The other classic types (mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted) differ in the reactive background, "but you don't need to know the difference between them otherwise." Nodular sclerosis Bands of fibrous (sclerotic) tissue surround nodules holding HRS cells and the reactive infiltrate Mixed cellularity The node is diffusely effaced; Reed-Sternberg cells are relatively frequent, in a mix of small lymphocytes, histiocytes, eosinophils and plasma cells; often EBV-associated Lymphocyte-rich Nodular or diffuse, with abundant small lymphocytes and virtually no neutrophils or eosinophils Lymphocyte-depleted Rare (2 percent or less); diffuse, with pleomorphic HRS cells; strongly associated with EBV His slide notes that subtyping may not matter for modern treatment, and he said you don't need the differences. The non-Hodgkin lymphomas, by contrast, more often start outside the nodes (DLBCL 30 to 40 percent of the time, Burkitt mostly, MALT lymphoma by definition) and are often widespread at diagnosis. Plasma cell neoplasms Plasma cells are the antibody-making end of the B-cell line, so their tumors, which he called B-cell neoplasms, make monoclonal immunoglobulin. He said they can be solitary, in one place, usually a rib or the spine, or multifocal, in the bone marrow, and may come with end-organ damage. Under the microscope the plasma cells have eccentric nuclei. A plasmacytoma is a solitary tumor of clonal plasma cells. Patients present with pain, swelling or a fracture at that spot, or with spinal cord compression. The standard treatment of an extramedullary plasmacytoma is radiation to the involved field. Plasma cell myeloma is a bone marrow-based, multifocal proliferation of plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is plasma cell myeloma, usually with a monoclonal immunoglobulin in the serum or urine, plus either organ damage from the disease or, without it, lab or imaging findings that predict organ damage within 2 years. It is considered incurable for most patients. He went through the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together ("it makes this sticky"). Aloud he listed the clinical findings as hypercalcemia, renal impairment and anemia, with the lytic bone; the CRAB chart on his slide is a picture. In the jaw, myeloma's lytic lesions are radiolucencies and its calcium is high, so it can look like the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism from Lecture A. The monoclonal protein, the rouleaux and the anemia point to myeloma. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma He skipped this slide ("I'm going to skip peripheral T-cell lymphoma"), giving only its gist: very aggressive T-cell lymphomas, whose markers say they are T cells, in patients who typically have B symptoms and don't necessarily respond to chemotherapy; the cells are large. The slide's detail follows. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL, NOS) is a mixed category: the mature T-cell lymphomas, in nodes or outside them, that don't fit a specific type. It is diagnosed nearly always in adults, and most present with advanced disease, usually lymphadenopathy and B symptoms, often with the marrow, liver, spleen, skin or GI tract involved. It carries T-cell markers, more often CD4 than CD8. These are aggressive lymphomas, with a poor response to therapy, frequent relapses and low survival. Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome He went through these quickly: "I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course." Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties. Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. He called it the aggressive version, with the blood and the nodes involved; the cerebriform nuclei in the blood help confirm it, and the node involvement can be subtle. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. He covered it briefly, as time ran short ("you guys may come across this"): EBV-associated lymphomas of the midline of the palate, perforating lesions from a very aggressive lymphoma causing necrosis. It occurs mainly in eastern Asia and among the Indigenous peoples of Central and South America, and is uncommon in Europe and the United States. The tumor grows diffusely around and into vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive), commonly with coagulative necrosis. With chemotherapy and radiotherapy, the 5-year survival in early-stage disease is over 70 percent. Chronic myeloid leukemia "The main chronic leukemia that you need to know is chronic myeloid leukemia." Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (the slides join the two names with a double colon), with too many neutrophils, a neutrophilic granulocytosis. At diagnosis, 90 to 95 percent carry the reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22), which makes the shortened chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia chromosome. The fusion gene makes a tyrosine kinase that is always on. Its increased activity is necessary and sufficient to cause the chronic phase, by keeping several signaling pathways switched on. Its phases. In the chronic phase, the neoplastic cells stay mostly in the blood, marrow, spleen and liver. More than 95 percent are diagnosed in the chronic phase, which comes on insidiously; some patients have no symptoms and are found on a routine blood count. Untreated, most progress within a few years to an advanced phase: declining health, fever and weight loss, and worse anemia, low platelets, a rising white count and a growing spleen. In the blast phase, blasts can infiltrate any site outside the marrow, especially the spleen, liver, lymph nodes, skin and soft tissues. Its blood and marrow. The white count is high, from 12,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter, with a median of about 80,000 (the slide writes it as 12 to 1,000 times 10 to the 9th per liter). The cells are mostly neutrophils at every stage of maturation, with peaks at the myelocytes and the segmented neutrophils, not blasts. He put it as the full pattern of maturation, from early blasts all the way to neutrophils, all increased in the blood and the marrow, with a count high enough to separate it from a reactive one, such as an infection. The marrow is hypercellular, more than 95 percent cellular, with granulocytes at every stage, and his slide shows small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. The karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome. Its treatment. Knowing the abnormal signal led to drugs that block it, the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, of which imatinib (Gleevec) was the first and is first-line therapy. It targets the enzymatically active part of the p210 BCR-ABL1 protein: it competes with ATP for the active site and so prevents the kinase from activating. He put it as blocking the binding site, so BCR-ABL1 can't bind its substrate and drive the cell to proliferate. In this era of kinase inhibitors, the most important sign of prognosis is the response to treatment, measured in the blood count, the chromosomes and the molecular test. Blasts and Auer rods "Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia." But they are not found only there. In lower numbers, under 20 percent, they appear in other myeloid disorders that can come before AML, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome. And outside the newborn period, blasts in the peripheral blood are always abnormal. An Auer rod is a red-blue, needle-like inclusion in the cytoplasm of some myeloblasts, formed from abnormal granules that fuse. Aloud he called them cytoplasmic inclusions of a myeloid blast. An Auer rod marks the blast as myeloid, which is why Auer rods exclude ALL. His slide adds that Auer rods are lysosomal and acid phosphatase-positive; textbooks (Robbins, the WHO) stress that they are myeloperoxidase-positive. He didn't mention either stain aloud, and no question asks. Acute promyelocytic leukemia He named two acute leukemias "you need to know", and this is the first. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a type of AML in which abnormal promyelocytes predominate. Its genetic hallmark is a balanced translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, t(15;17), which fuses the promyelocytic leukemia gene, PML, with the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene, RARA. The fusion protein, PML-RARA (written with a double colon on the slides), causes the disease by impairing myeloid differentiation: maturation stops at the promyelocyte. The cells look the part: abnormal promyelocytes whose cytoplasm is packed with large, dense granules staining bright pink, red or purple, and distinctive cells holding bundles of Auer rods scattered through the cytoplasm. He showed numerous Auer rods in them. He gave two reasons to know it. The danger: "they have certain clinical presentations that can kill the patient." APL is frequently associated with a coagulopathy and a risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which can cause early death: "you clot everywhere at the same time, which makes you at risk of clotting and bleeding." In the mouth, that means bleeding gums, petechiae and bruising. The good news, "the treatment for it is excellent compared to other acute leukemias": all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide (ATRA plus ATO), without conventional chemotherapy, is highly effective and largely curative for low- and intermediate-risk APL. The retinoic acid lets the blocked promyelocytes mature. Acute monocytic leukemia and the gums The second acute leukemia he said you need: "the thing that I want you to know is that they can have extramedullary disease presentation in the oral cavity." Acute monocytic leukemia is an AML with monocytic differentiation and no defining genetic abnormality. The marrow is extensively infiltrated by immature, intermediate-sized to large cells with irregularly lobulated to kidney-shaped (reniform) nuclei, fine chromatin and distinct nucleoli. Flow cytometry shows two or more monocytic markers. Patients present with symptoms of their cytopenias, with disease outside the marrow, or both, and the oral cavity is one of those places. AML that forms a mass outside the marrow is called a myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML). In the mouth it shows as gingival hypertrophy: swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells. His slides cite two case reports, one of them a myeloid sarcoma of the mandibular gingiva that was the relapse of a treated AML. This is what his objective means by the extramedullary presentation of acute leukemia. He said a biopsy of those gums can look a little like lymphoma, but studies confirm the leukemia, and the marrow is diffusely full of blasts. Swollen gums in a patient who is tired, pale and bruising call for a blood count. B-lymphoblastic leukemia For B-ALL and T-ALL he said: "You don't need to know a ton of detail other than some of the demographic information for this." They occur mostly in children, the most common acute leukemia of childhood, though they can occur in adults. The diagnosis doesn't strictly need 20 percent blasts if other features, such as the cytogenetics, make it, and most children do well, after the testing sorts them by risk. The rest of this section is from his slides. B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL, also called precursor B-cell ALL) is a neoplasm of precursor lymphoid cells committed to the B-cell line. When it involves the marrow, and usually the blood, it is B-ALL; when nodes or other tissues are the primary sites, it is B-lymphoblastic lymphoma. It is diagnosed by morphology and flow cytometry (the blasts essentially always carry B-lineage antigens) and classified further by its cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities, which carry prognostic and treatment implications. No set blast number is required, although a diagnosis with under 20 percent blasts is made with caution. B-ALL occurs mainly in children: 75 percent of patients are under 6, and it is the most common leukemia of childhood. The incidence is bimodal, with a second, smaller peak in the fifth decade of life (the 40s). It usually presents with bone marrow failure: low platelets, anemia, low neutrophils, or all three. The lymphoblasts range from small cells with scant cytoplasm to larger ones with more pale blue-gray cytoplasm, sometimes vacuolated. With risk-stratified treatment, more than 90 percent of children reach long-term remission; adults do less well, because of harsher biology and the toxicity of treatment. T-lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoma T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is the same idea in the T-cell line: he said the testing confirms the cells are T cells, and the outcomes are a little worse than B-ALL's, but still generally good. The lymphoblasts have a very high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and the involved marrow looks very blue. It is called T-ALL when the blood and marrow are the primary sites and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LBL) when the primary site is a lymph node, the mediastinum (thymus) or another tissue such as the skin, tonsils, liver, spleen, CNS or testes. Again, no set blast number is required, with caution under 20 percent. T-ALL typically brings a high white count, often with a large mediastinal mass; lymphadenopathy and an enlarged liver and spleen are common. T-LBL often presents as a rapidly growing anterior mediastinal mass, sometimes as a respiratory emergency. Its lymphoblasts are indistinguishable under the microscope from those of B-ALL: flow cytometry, showing T-lineage antigens, tells them apart. Long-term response rates approach 85 percent in children and adolescents and 60 percent in adults. When acute leukemia comes from something else He said some patients develop acute leukemia de novo, with no precursor lesion, but others first have a pre-neoplastic myeloid disorder, such as myelodysplastic syndrome, or CML, which can eventually become an acute leukemia. On his slide: acute leukemia, or a blast phase, can be the final stage of another marrow disorder, the result of treatment for a different cancer, or linked to a genetic disorder. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more. CML and CMML (chronic myelomonocytic leukemia). The myeloproliferative neoplasms, with persistently high counts: polycythemia vera (increased red cells), essential thrombocythemia (increased platelets) and primary myelofibrosis (fibrosis in the marrow). Myeloid neoplasm after cytotoxic therapy: after alkylating agents and/or ionizing radiation (type 1) or after topoisomerase II inhibitors (type 2). It generally arises within 10 years of the last exposure and has a bad prognosis. Myeloid proliferations of Down syndrome: two clonal conditions of children with trisomy 21, transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome. Treating acute leukemia Treatment of acute leukemia has two objectives: eradicate the leukemic cell mass, with cytoreductive chemotherapy, radiotherapy and marrow transplant, and provide supportive care. The goal is complete remission: no leukemia-related signs or symptoms, no demonstrable disease, and the return of marrow function, with the blood's granulocyte, platelet and red cell values back to normal. The translocations side by side Five translocations run through this lecture, and they are easy to swap. These are the molecular associations he said you need: "You do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined." t(14;18) IGH and BCL2 Follicular lymphoma (85 to 90 percent) BCL2 always on, so the cells don't die t(11;14) Cyclin D1 and IGH Mantle cell lymphoma (at least 95 percent) Cyclin D1 on; the cyclin D1 stain is diagnostic t(8;14) MYC and IGH Burkitt lymphoma (80 percent) MYC on: very fast growth t(9;22) BCR and ABL1 (the Philadelphia chromosome) CML (90 to 95 percent) A tyrosine kinase always on; blocked by imatinib t(15;17) PML and RARA Acute promyelocytic leukemia Maturation stops at the promyelocyte; treated with retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide A memory hook: the three B-cell lymphomas all move a gene next to IGH on chromosome 14: BCL2 from 18 (follicular), cyclin D1 from 11 (mantle cell), MYC from 8 (Burkitt). The two myeloid ones are fusions: BCR with ABL1 in CML, PML with RARA in APL.
